eyebrow: Statistics & Probability for Data Science · Chapter 3, Lesson 12
subtitle: The bell curve — symmetric, peaked, set by just two numbers.

code:
from scipy import stats
d = stats.norm(loc=40, scale=5)
print(round(d.cdf(45), 4))              # 0.8413 -- 45 min or less
print(round(d.cdf(45) - d.cdf(35), 4))  # 0.6827 -- within 1 sd
print(round(d.sf(50), 4))               # 0.0228 -- more than 50 min
caption: loc is the mean, scale is the standard deviation -- NOT the variance.
Real matplotlib/scipy output: shaded bands at 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations from the mean.

code:
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    print(k, round(stats.norm.cdf(k) - stats.norm.cdf(-k), 4))
# 1  0.6827
# 2  0.9545
# 3  0.9973
caption: ppf, the inverse of cdf, answers percentile questions: 95% of deliveries finish by ~48.2 min.

eyebrow: Z-scores: a common scale across units
code:
z = (52 - 40) / 5
print(z, round(stats.norm.sf(z), 4))   # 2.4  0.0082

stats.norm.ppf(0.975)   # ~1.96 -- where 95% intervals come from
caption: A 52-minute delivery is 2.4 sd above average -- only ~0.8% of deliveries are that slow.

eyebrow: Does real data actually look normal?
code:
s = rng.normal(40, 5, size=10_000)
inside1 = (abs(s - s.mean()) < s.std(ddof=1)).mean()
print(round(inside1, 4))   # 0.6792 -- close to the theoretical 0.6827
caption: Normal sample skew ~0.007; a right-skewed exponential sample gave 1.866 -- check, don't assume.
